The Peacocks of Sri Lanka: More than just a beautiful bird

From unexpected encounters on the road to ancient Buddhist stories and religious traditions, discover the special place peacocks hold in Sri Lanka.

The first time I realised that peacocks were going to become part of my Sri Lankan memories was before I had even reached my destination.

I had just landed in Colombo, climbed into a taxi and begun the journey south towards Tangalle. As we travelled along the expressway, I noticed large yellow warning signs alerting drivers to peacocks on
the road.

Peacocks? On the road?

That was certainly not something I expected to see on my first day in
Sri Lanka.

But the island had more surprises waiting for me.

Morning coffee with unexpected visitors

For the first three days of my trip, I stayed in Rekawa, a quieter
coastal area surrounded by tropical greenery and mangroves.

My mornings had a simple rhythm: wake up, make coffee and enjoy the peaceful surroundings. And then, quite casually,
peacocks would wander through
the garden.

They did not seem particularly interested in me. They simply walked around, exploring their surroundings as if sharing the garden with me was the most ordinary thing in the world.

I watched them, filmed them and found myself smiling at how naturally they belonged there. It was such a beautiful contrast to the unfamiliar places I had travelled through to get there.

Later, during a safari, I encountered another magnificent peacock. This time, a male stepped onto the road and spread his spectacular train, displaying the shimmering green and blue feathers that make this bird so recognisable.

It was one of those moments when you instinctively reach for your camera, hoping to preserve at least a little of what you
are seeing.

I encountered peacocks so often that they gradually became part of my personal picture of Sri Lanka, alongside elephants and the island’s beautiful coconut palms.

Perhaps that is what makes a place memorable. Sometimes, it is not only the famous landmarks or the experiences we carefully plan. It is also a bird walking through a garden while we drink our morning coffee, or an unexpected encounter in the middle of a safari road.

Only later did I begin to appreciate how much meaning this bird carries beyond its
striking appearance.

A bird that belongs to
the island

The Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus) is native to Sri Lanka and other parts of South Asia. Although many people associate peacocks with ornamental gardens and royal estates, they are also part of the island’s natural wildlife.

In Sri Lanka, they are particularly associated with the dry lowlands, where open grassland and scrub provide food and shelter. They can also be found around cultivated land and human settlements, which helps explain why visitors sometimes encounter them in gardens or
near roads.

That first warning sign on my journey south suddenly made much more sense.

Peacocks and traffic sometimes meet along the Southern Expressway. Research conducted on a section of the expressway has documented collisions involving peafowl, highlighting the risks roads can pose to wildlife.

Those warning signs are therefore more than a curiosity for travellers. They are a reminder to drive carefully and give
wildlife space.

For me, seeing peacocks so frequently around Rekawa made the experience especially personal. Rather than spotting one briefly from a distance, I had the chance to watch them going about their everyday lives.

There is something wonderful about seeing a wild animal in its own surroundings, without a performance, a fence or a carefully arranged
photo opportunity.

The male’s extravagant train may capture our attention first, but the quieter moments can be just as memorable.

The peacock in
Buddhist storytelling

The peacock also has a place in Buddhist storytelling, including the Jātaka tales, which recount stories of the Buddha’s previous births.

One of these is the Mora Jātaka, often known as the Peacock Jātaka. In this story, the Bodhisattva is born as a beautiful golden peacock living in the wilderness.

The peacock recites protective verses associated with the sun and the Buddhas. For many years, hunters sent to capture him are unsuccessful. Eventually, a hunter uses a peahen to distract him. The peacock is caught, but his story does not
end there.

Brought before a king, he speaks about virtue and the impermanence of life. He challenges the idea that eating his flesh could make someone immortal, explaining that even he, despite his extraordinary qualities, must one day die. Moved by his words, the king allows him to return to

the wilderness.

A related tale, the Mahā-Mora Jātaka, also features a captured peacock whose wisdom changes the behaviour of those around him.

These stories offer more than an explanation of why the peacock is admired.
They use the bird to explore deeper themes, including desire, self-restraint, morality and the consequences of our choices.

This is one of the fascinating things about traditional storytelling: an animal we might first notice for its appearance can become a way of reflecting on
human behaviour.

The Mora Jātaka belongs to a wider Buddhist literary tradition and is not unique to Sri Lanka. Nevertheless, it offers a meaningful connection when exploring the place of the peacock in the island’s religious and cultural imagination.

The peacock and Kataragama

Another important connection appears in the worship of Kataragama Deviyo, a deity revered by different religious communities in Sri Lanka.

Kataragama is a significant pilgrimage destination associated with the Hindu god Skanda, also widely known as Murugan. The traditions surrounding the deity bring together elements of Hindu and Buddhist devotion, alongside other local beliefs
and practices.

In Hindu iconography, Skanda or Murugan is commonly depicted with a peacock as his mount. This association is also reflected in Sri Lankan religious traditions linked
to Kataragama.

The peacock’s presence extends beyond religious imagery and into traditional performance. Sri Lanka’s Kandyan dance tradition includes the Mayura Wannama, a dance inspired by the peacock. Through movement, rhythm and gesture, performers evoke the bird’s distinctive appearance and graceful behaviour.

It is a beautiful example of how the natural world can inspire artistic expression and
devotional practice.

The peacock’s beauty is visible to anyone who sees it. Its cultural meaning, however, is shaped by the stories, traditions and communities through which it

is understood.

Beauty, pride and the language of feathers

It is easy to understand why the peacock has become a symbol of beauty and majesty in
many cultures.

Its iridescent blue neck, intricate feather patterns and spectacular train make it one of the most visually distinctive birds in the region. When a male opens his train, the familiar eye-like markings create a display that seems almost too elaborate to be real.

Across South Asian art and storytelling, peacocks have inspired images of elegance, dignity and splendour. Their forms also appear in decorative art and religious imagery.

But beauty can carry more than
one meaning.

In everyday language, comparing someone to a peacock can suggest elegance, confidence and pride. In other contexts, it can imply vanity or excessive self-importance. The same striking display that makes the bird magnificent can also become a metaphor for showing off.

Perhaps that contradiction is part of the peacock’s enduring appeal. It can represent beauty worth admiring, but it can also remind us how easily admiration can turn into vanity.

Of course, not every image of a peacock carries the same symbolism. Meanings vary between traditions, stories and individual works of art.

Still, the bird’s unmistakable presence makes it a powerful subject for expressing colour, movement, grace and grandeur.

Folklore, wildlife and the importance of protection

Traditional beliefs about peacocks can be found across South Asia. Some connect their calls and displays with approaching rain or changing seasons. Others associate them with protection and the triumph of good over evil.

Another familiar belief links the peacock with snakes and poison. Peafowl do sometimes eat small snakes, but in folklore this behaviour can take on a wider symbolic meaning, representing the overcoming of danger or the defeat of evil.

Such interpretations belong to the world of folklore and symbolism rather than being scientific explanations of animal behaviour. They offer a glimpse into how people have interpreted and found meaning in the natural world over generations.

But peacocks are living animals, not simply symbols. Their survival depends on the landscapes they inhabit and the choices people make around them.

The warning signs I saw on the expressway now seem to carry an additional meaning. They tell drivers to watch for peacocks, but they also reveal something about the island itself: wildlife is not always separated from everyday life by the boundaries of a national park or a designated
viewing area.

Sometimes, nature is right there beside us, crossing the road we are travelling on.

And that makes our responsibility to respect it all the more important.

A little piece of Sri Lanka that stayed with me

When I think back to my time in Sri Lanka, I remember the elephants, the coconut palms, the ocean and the warmth of the island. But I also remember

those peacocks.

I remember the unexpected road signs on the way south from Colombo. I remember sitting with my morning coffee in Rekawa while they wandered through the garden. And I remember the male who spread his train during the safari, turning an ordinary stretch of road into an
unforgettable moment.

I did not travel to Sri Lanka specifically to see peacocks. I had no idea they would become such a familiar part of my journey.

Perhaps that is why these encounters mean so much to me. They were not something I had planned or put on an itinerary. They simply happened, again and again, until the peacock became part of the way I remember the island.

The bird can be admired for its beauty, explored through Buddhist stories, recognised in religious traditions and celebrated in dance. Yet none of those meanings fully replaces the experience of seeing one in the wild.

Sometimes, a peacock is simply a peacock, walking through a garden in the early
morning sunshine.

And sometimes, that is more than enough to make you fall a little more in love with
a place.

For me, the peacock will always be one of the living colours of Sri Lanka: unexpected, graceful and impossible
to forget.
